title: character-naming agent skill (jwynia)
rule: Draw names from curated lists with real randomisation, not from the model. Swapping Chen for Kim or Patel is still 'median-hopping': a corrected model cycles to the top name of each ethnic cluster. Use whole cultural naming packages (given name and surname from one tradition) and fix period, age cohort, region, generation (immigrant or second generation) and class before choosing.
example: Flagged as over-used: surnames Chen, Patel, Garcia, Kim; first names Maya, Marcus, Sofia, Aiden. Source is one skill's docs, not a measurement; 'Sarah Chen' appears only as a sample command there.
llm_tell: Chen/Patel/Garcia/Kim surnames; Maya, Marcus, Sofia, Aiden first names; correction swaps to the next ethnicity's modal name (unmeasured claim)

title: Personal names around the world (W3C i18n, Richard Ishida)
rule: Names differ in structure: family name first (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Hungarian), patronymics (Icelandic -son/-dottir, Malay bin/binti), gender-inflected Russian patronymics and surnames, two family names in Spanish and Brazilian names, Thai everyday nicknames, Vietnamese addressed by given name, Indian names that may carry village or caste, a middle initial that means mother's maiden name in the Philippines. A character from such a culture should follow its structure and form of address, not 'first name, last name'.
example: Icelanders are listed and addressed by given name; Spanish names carry paternal then maternal surname.
llm_tell: Treating every name as given+surname, western order, one surname

title: How to find the perfect name (David Placek, Lexicon Branding, Lenny's Newsletter)
rule: Descriptive names blend into the field; invented or surprising words signal something new. Aim for trust plus imagination, an original idea, and ease of processing from familiar parts. Generate 1,000+ ideas and shortlist 50 to 100. Decide how the name should sound (fast, full, reliable) before naming. Groups of four or more brainstorming together give marginal results through peer pressure. Test with customers and multi-market research. Paywalled 'what not to do' section not read.
example: Swiffer chosen over 80% of the time in preference tests; BlackBerry presented beside safer ProMail, EasyMail, DynaMail; Pentium researched in six markets; Navan, Outback, Dasani.
llm_tell: A model asked for brand names returns a short list of descriptive or smooshed compounds; volume of 1,000 ideas is a human-process norm

title: BrandingMag: The Science of Sound Symbolism and the Importance of Your Brand Name (Lexicon)
rule: Sound carries meaning: obstruents (t, k, b) read hard, fast, reliable; sonorants (n, l, m) read soft, smooth; V reads vibrant. Lexicon tests with paired nonsense-word questionnaires (which invented word is faster, more dependable, fits the angular shape). Vendor material, secondhand through a search summary.
example: BlackBerry, T-Mobile, BlackRock (b/t reliability); Corvette, Vercel (V).

title: Types of brand names (Fabrik Brands) and similar agency taxonomies
rule: Agency taxonomy: descriptive (clear, SEO-friendly, hard to trademark), evocative or suggestive (Nike, Apple), invented or portmanteau (Kodak; most legal room, costs money to teach), founder names. Pick the type first, then generate. The Igor naming guide itself was not found or read; this is the generic substitute.

title: How Chartbeat's data scientists came up with the single greatest headline
rule: Over 100 publishers and 10,000 tests: demonstrative adjectives ('this', 'these') were the one clear winner; articles ('a', 'an', 'the') lowered scaled click-through; headlines of 73+ characters raised it; numbers raised the chance of winning but not CTR significantly; questions, short punchy headlines (32 characters or fewer) and name-dropping showed no significant effect. Testing five variants gave a winner about 50% above average against about 23% for two. Results vary by publisher; test your own.
example: 'this' / 'these' in the headline beat the same story without it.
llm_tell: Not measured; the finding is that punchy-short and question headlines, which models favour, have no demonstrated edge

title: Negative words in news headlines generate more clicks (Nieman Lab on the Upworthy Research Archive study)
rule: About 22,743 Upworthy A/B tests (2013 to 2015, about 105,000 headline variants, 370 million impressions): each extra negative word in a headline of average length raised click-through by 2.3%, positive words lowered it, and sad words beat angry or fearful ones. Measures clicks on one outlet in one era, not whether the headline is good or honest.
example: Sadness-laden beat anger, fear and joy.
llm_tell: Models default to upbeat, positive-valence headlines, the opposite of what this dataset rewarded (inference, not measured on LLMs)

title: None of your headline writing tricks work, except this one (Poynter, on the Chartbeat data)
rule: Secondhand summary of the Chartbeat data: most headline tricks showed no reliable effect. Nieman Lab's note on 141,000 tests across 293 sites adds that A/B results optimise one story and do not extrapolate.

title: Laissez-Faire Harms: Algorithmic Biases in Generative Language Models
rule: Infers race from first names in LLM-written stories: models omit non-White characters from neutral prompts and place them in subordinate roles once power is added. Measures representation, not which names recur; no frequency table of names found.
llm_tell: Default casts lean toward a narrow set of names; no direct name-frequency measurement of 'Sarah Chen' or 'Marcus' found (null)

title: SSA Popular Baby Names
topic: realistic contemporary names by birth year
rule: Fetch returned 403, so the page was not read. A search summary says SSA lists the top names for each birth year back to 1880, by state, from card applications at birth: look up the character's birth year, not today's list. US Census surname files and UK ONS data were not reached.
